data.name: The Amber Throne
data.detailed_description:
After awakening from her coffin, Arra recalls little but the last words spoken by her father, “Destroy the Amber Throne.” Looking into the sky, she finds what was once his magnificent castle is now floating in the sky, far above the world below. Arra must find a way to reach the castle before others catch wind of it, lest the powerful Amber Throne fall into the wrong hands.

Amber Throne is a traditional JRPG-styled game that focuses on turn-based battling and some light exploration. The game features a large cast of unique monsters that change stances depending on actions taken during combat, and a party with mostly mixed hybrid roles to deal with them. Learning monster behavior and how your skills affect them is essential to reaching victory.

  • Fully painted world with diverse settings and unique characters.

  • Many monsters with multiple stances and behaviors to master.

  • Five party members each with their own skills and advantages.

  • Crafting for the game's best equipment and items.
  • 12-15 hour-long story with optional content and exploration.

The game is a bit more atmospheric and ambient than most JRPG-styled games, with emphasis on theme and mood, hopefully making it feel a bit different to experience!

Controls

Shift to Run

Arrow Keys to Move

Z / Enter to Confirm

X / Esc For Main Menu Or Cancel

F5 For Fullscreen

D+hold For Skipping Dialogue

reviews.review:
Haven't finished the game yet, but I can already recommend it. The main reason is, it's a work of art. Now, some people will read that as me claiming it's a masterpiece 10/10 GOAT of a game, but that's not what I mean; it has flaws, it has limitations, it's built from RPGMaker, so no, it's not revolutionary. But it IS art; the looks, the music, the story--it is a unique, engaging experience that a creative and thoughtful person poured himself into. Contrast this to most RPGMaker titles; typically, they are made by fans of the genre who, unfortunately, have very little originality or imagination, and so make incredibly basic, generic, derivative products, or frustrating half-finished ones. And that's not even talking about the outright scams in the field. No, this is what indie gaming is really supposed to be; it has some rough edges, it's not the size of a Dragon Quest game, but it's a product someone truly cared about. What would you rather have; a cheap, inferior copy of the Mona Lisa, or an original painting by a fairly good, but not amazing, painter? The closest comparison I can think of to this game is, despite the wild differences in style and tone and all that, is Fear and Hunger--both games are one person's vision brought to life. 

As an actual game, it's fine. I like the skill system--you can see all available skills for a character from the start and so deliberately work towards the ones you want to use. The game tries to keep things fresh by having various skills or effects actually alter enemies; a defense-breaking move on a guy with a shield will basically transform him into a guy without a shield, and this can change not only the defense rating but also which damage types the enemy is strong/weak against, as well as which moves he will use (one move might actually be raising his shield, restoring his defense buff and healing himself). Buffing and debuffing is pretty notable in it's effectiveness. The game avoids the basic character archetypes; you don't get a tank, healer, mage, and DPS. It's a good idea to try to spread out your skills to have a range of options with your characters; different buffs, debuffs, status effect-infliction, and damage types, so you don't run into enemies you can't effectively fight. Equipment isn't just "grab the highest-attack weapon and highest-defense armor." No, some gear doesn't raise defense at all, because it raises other stats; skills will all show you which stats are used in the damage calculation, and you can see why it might be worth sacrificing defense for boosts elsewhere...but don't take that too far either, because healing isn't quite as easy as most JRPGs (well, items are fairly simple, but you probably don't want to spend the money to buy hundreds of potions). 

I have yet to encounter the game-breaking bugs I see other users mention; doesn't mean they don't exist, just that this isn't a Bethesda game where you are lucky to go an hour without something horrible happening. You have 3 save slots and an auto-save--remember the gamer mantra of "Save early, save often" instead of relying 100% on the auto-save, and it shouldn't be too big of a deal even if you do run into a bug. There are no save points though; you can save anywhere, at nearly anytime, so there shouldn't be a huge issue. You can also backtrack in most cases, especially since enemies don't respawn, so if you're beat up and don't want to use all your healing items, just trek back to town to rest. 

Overall, yes, it plays like an RPGMaker title, one of the better ones. But that is couched in a lovely presentation with an interesting story and world that elevates it above other, fairly generic competitors. Doesn't seem the creator is making games anymore, unless he got into an actual studio somewhere as a professional, and that's a shame. I recommend any fans of the genre pick this up; it may not be your favorite game, but it certainly won't be a forgettable, flavor-of-the-week experience.
